question: What revenue threshold puts a company in scope of California SB 253?

passages.title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
passages.text: 8. California SB 253 and SB 261. Two companion laws administered by the California Air Resources Board (CARB). Components: SB 253 (Climate Corporate Data Accountability Act) requires annual Scope 1 and 2 emissions reporting from 2026 and Scope 3 from 2027, measured under the GHG Protocol, with third-party assurance phasing from limited to reasonable. SB 261 (Climate-Related Financial Risk Act) requires a biennial public report on climate-related financial risk and mitigation, which may follow TCFD or ISSB. In scope: US-organized entities doing business in California with total annual revenue above $1bn (SB 253) or above $500m (SB 261), public or private, measured globally (Persefoni). Status: CARB moved the first SB 253 deadline from 10 August to 10 November 2026 and will not require assurance on that first report (Baker Tilly). A Ninth Circuit injunction has paused SB 261 enforcement since November 2025; a ruling on the First Amendment challenge was still pending as of August 2026. Enforcement: CARB administrative penalties of up to $500,000 per reporting year under SB 253 and up to $50,000 under SB 261. Scope 3 misstatements are protected by a safe harbor if made in good faith, and penalties for Scope 3 are limited to non-filing until 2030.

passages.title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
passages.text: 3. GHG Protocol. The accounting rulebook for emissions that every regime in this briefing relies on. Components: Corporate Standard, Scope 2 Guidance (location- and market-based methods) and Scope 3 Standard (15 value chain categories). A revision under consultation would require hourly and regional matching of renewable energy certificates for market-based Scope 2 claims, with a final standard expected in 2027 and implementation likely from 2028 (Greenplaces). In scope: Voluntary; referenced directly by California SB 253, ISSB, AASB S2 and ESRS. Enforcement: None of its own; errors are penalized through the laws that reference it.

passages.title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
passages.text: 7. Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD). A conduct obligation, not only a disclosure one. Components: Identify, prevent and remediate adverse human rights and environmental impacts in the company's own operations and chain of activities, with a risk-based focus. In scope: EU companies with more than 5,000 employees and EUR 1.5bn net worldwide turnover, and non-EU companies with EUR 1.5bn EU turnover. Compliance is required from 26 July 2029 (Morrison Foerster). Enforcement: National supervisory authorities with administrative fines; the Omnibus narrowed the liability and penalty provisions (Accountancy Europe).
passages.location: p.3, "7. Corporate Sustainability Due Diligence Directive (CSDDD)"

passages.title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
passages.text: 9. Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards (AASB S2). Mandatory climate reporting under Chapter 2M of the Corporations Act 2001, based on IFRS S2. Components: A sustainability report lodged with the annual report, covering governance, strategy, risk management and metrics; Scope 1 and 2 emissions from year one and Scope 3 from year two; scenario analysis at 1.5°C and at 2.5°C or higher; a directors' declaration; assurance phasing from limited to reasonable. AASB S1 (general sustainability) is voluntary. In scope: Entities that lodge annual reports and meet two of three size tests, phased by group. Group 1 began with years starting 1 January 2025 (revenue A$500m, assets A$1bn, 500 employees). Group 2 began with years starting 1 July 2026 (A$200m, A$500m, 250 employees). Group 3 follows from 1 July 2027 (A$50m, A$25m, 100 employees) (Carbon Impact). Large emitters under the National Greenhouse and Energy Reporting Act and large asset owners are also caught. Enforcement: ASIC, under the same civil penalty and director liability provisions as financial reports. A three-year "modified liability" period limits claims over Scope 3, scenario analysis and transition plans to ASIC-only actions (Naturaliste).
passages.location: p.4, "9. Australian Sustainability Reporting Standards (AASB S2)"

passages.title: Global Sustainability Reporting Briefing
passages.section: 4. Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS
passages.text: 4. Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS. The EU's mandatory sustainability reporting law and its technical standards. Components: Double materiality (impacts on people and planet, plus financial risk); 2 cross-cutting and 10 topical ESRS; mandatory limited assurance; digital tagging, now postponed. Revised ESRS adopted on 3 July 2026 cut mandatory datapoints by over 60% and total datapoints by over 70% (European Commission). In scope: EU companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450m net turnover. Non-EU groups are in scope with over EUR 450m EU turnover and an EU subsidiary or branch above EUR 200m (Latham & Watkins). Suppliers under 1,000 employees can decline data requests beyond a voluntary SME standard. Enforcement: Penalties set by each Member State; statutory auditors or accredited assurers sign off; national market regulators supervise listed issuers.
passages.location: p.2, "4. Corporate Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) and ESRS"

answer: US-organized entities doing business in California with total annual revenue above $1bn are in scope for SB 253 [1].
